summary:
Abia lies within Nigeria's uniform criminal framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationwide and reaches visitors as well as residents, carrying up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct. The statute reaches beyond marriage: it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years, and police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sharia criminal law does not reach Abia. It operates only in the twelve northern states, where male sodomy can carry the death penalty under state Zina provisions; Abia is a southern state, so the federal penalties and the national arrest climate apply here in full without that religious layer.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025) sets out the entry-level exposure. Same-sex sexual acts between men carry up to 14 years' imprisonment under secular law. Entering a same-sex marriage or civil union is punishable by 14 years, and a further 10 years falls on anyone who administers, witnesses, abets or aides the solemnization of one, or who supports the registration, operation and sustenance of gay clubs, societies, organisations, processions or meetings.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in the seat of national government hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) separately documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing, a direct hazard for visitors using dating apps.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by SaharaReporters on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states, and of liability for those who help arrange or attend a same-sex wedding.
tangentialFactors:
A 2022 federal court ruling struck down sections of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act as unconstitutional, yet the 14-year framework remains the operative baseline in every other source consulted, and no source states which sections survived or how the ruling changed charging practice.

The UK Home Office note records tens of LGBT+ arrests per year across Nigeria, alongside police and Islamic-police harassment that includes beatings, blackmail, extortion and torture. It also records at least four sharia death sentences imposed since 2022, none of which have been carried out.

Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law that produces a climate of hostility independent of its text, which is why the practical risk in a southern state such as Abia does not collapse to the statutory penalty alone.

The comparison with the northern states is stark but not transferable: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara operate sharia criminal law for Muslims, and Abia is not among them.
localsOnly:
Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and residents of Abia live under the same arrest climate documented nationally, including community hostility that operates independently of any single prosecution.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024.

Press coverage at Bobrisky's sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to official discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Registration, operation or participation in gay clubs, societies and organisations is itself an offence under the national statute, and public displays of same-sex amorous relationships are separately punishable, which constrains organising and visible community life inside Abia as much as anywhere else in Nigeria.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

No Abia-specific arrest, prosecution or enforcement data is sourced; the state-level picture is inferred from national and UK government material, and the frequency of enforcement inside Abia itself is unresolved.

The scope and practical effect of the 2022 federal court ruling striking down sections of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act is unresolved: no source consulted identifies which sections fell or how prosecutors have responded since.

No sourced record addresses how the Nigerian Correctional Service now assigns placement for trans detainees generally, beyond the single finding on the Bobrisky case, and no source documents trans-specific legal protections or a complaint mechanism available to visitors in Abia.
